title: Risk Vocabulary, One Word Apart
blurb: Six governance and risk-analysis pairs the exam loves to swap for each other. One flipped detail tells them apart every time.
source: Chapple CISSP SG 10ed ch.1, ch.2 · April-2024 outline 1.6, 1.9

pairs.dimension: risk before controls vs risk left after controls

a.text: Before any safeguards are designed, the assessment team scores the warehouse's exposure to fire exactly as the building stands today, with no sprinklers and no controls assumed.
a.why: Scoring the environment as it exists prior to any risk management effort is the starting-point measurement — the same fire exposure, once controls are in place, gets a different name.

b.text: After sprinklers, fire doors, and a suppression contract are installed, the team scores what fire exposure the warehouse still carries.
b.why: What remains once safeguards have already been applied — the gap management is left to accept or treat further — is measured after the fact, never before controls exist.

pairs.dimension: the danger itself vs the weakness it exploits

a.text: A ransomware crew has publicly stated it is actively targeting hospitals that run unpatched imaging servers this quarter.
a.why: A potential source of harm to an asset — the actor or event capable of causing damage — is what this side names, independent of whether the target has any weakness to exploit.

b.text: The hospital's imaging server has been running an unpatched OS build for eleven months, with the vendor's fix sitting unapplied.
b.why: The flaw or absence of a safeguard in the asset itself, which a threat could exploit, is the other half — a weakness can exist even with no attacker currently pursuing it.

pairs.dimension: the possible harm vs the combined likelihood-and-impact it produces

a.text: A disgruntled former administrator whose credentials were never revoked is a known danger to the payroll database.
a.why: Naming the potential source of harm on its own, before it is combined with how exploitable the target is or what damage would follow, keys this side.

b.text: Given that the same administrator's credentials are still active on an unmonitored VPN account, the payroll database's likelihood and impact of unauthorized access this quarter is assessed as high.
b.why: Combining a threat with the vulnerability it can exploit into a measured likelihood and severity of harm is the calculation this side performs — a threat alone is only one input to it.

pairs.dimension: mandatory intent from leadership vs mandatory specific requirement

a.text: Senior management publishes a one-page document stating that all customer data must be encrypted, without naming any algorithm or key length.
a.why: A high-level, management-issued statement of intent and scope — mandatory, but silent on implementation detail — is what this side captures; the specifics live one level down.

b.text: A companion document mandates AES-256 with a 90-day key rotation for every system that stores customer data.
b.why: A specific, compulsory requirement that makes an upstream policy's intent uniformly enforceable across the organization is this side's role — it says exactly what, where the policy only said that.

pairs.dimension: compulsory uniform requirement vs optional recommended approach

a.text: Every laptop in the fleet must have full-disk encryption switched on before IT hands it to its user, and no team may opt out.
a.why: The same control, stated as a compulsory requirement applied uniformly with no discretion left to the implementer, is what defines this side.

b.text: A companion document advises switching full-disk encryption on before a laptop is handed over, while noting a team may substitute an equivalent protection where that suits its workflow better.
b.why: The identical control, offered as advice with substitution permitted, is the other half — a recommendation that can be adapted locally, never an enforced rule.

a.text: The team calculates that a server outage has a single loss expectancy of $40,000 and an annualized rate of occurrence of 0.5, giving an annualized loss expectancy of $20,000.
a.why: Assigning real dollar figures derived from mathematical calculation, such as SLE and ARO feeding an ALE, is this side's method.

b.text: Unable to price the outage precisely, the same team instead has stakeholders rank it 'high' impact and 'likely' frequency on a workshop scorecard, based on their judgment and experience.
b.why: Subjective, scenario-driven ranking using judgment and intuition rather than dollar calculations is the other half of the pair, used when the figures aren't available or precise.
